list.listitem: Ultrasound is the best initial diagnostic test for cholecystitis; scintigraphy with hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) can be obtained if ultrasound results are negative or equivocal. B
Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (within 72 hours) for acute cholecystitis is recommended. A
If a patient is too sick or high risk to undergo surgery, a cholecystotomy tube is the next best choice. A

background.definition: Acute cholecystitis (AC) is acute gallbladder inflammation and it occurs usually when gallstones obstructs the cystic duct.

list.listitem: Acute cholecystitis is diagnosed in approximately 200 000 people in the US each year.
During the COVID-19 first wave pandemic in Spain, a 1/3 reduction in the number of mild cases treated for acute surgical inflammatory process including cholecystitis was observed.

Acute cholecystitis (AC) is the most frequent complication of gallstones and occurs in 10% to 30% of patients requiring cholecystectomy. Most patients with gallstones do not develop symptoms; AC develops in up to 10% of patients with symptomatic gallstones. .
Acute acalculous cholecystitis accounts for 10% of cases of AC. The incidence is higher in intensive care populations, particularly patients in burn and trauma units.
More than 20 million Americans are estimated to have gallstones, with approximately 300,000 cholecystectomies performed annually.

Data from NY State showed 711,406 cholecystectomies were performed from 1995 to 2013, of which 637,308 (89.58 %) were laparoscopic. 72.81% of cholecystectomies were performed for calculous cholecystitis (n = 464,032). Outpatient laparascopic surgery incidence increased to 48.6 % in 2013.
Acute cholecystitis can develop in patients with and without gallstones.

Calculus cholecystitis is caused by a cystic duct obstruction or passage of gallstones into the gallbladder neck, which causes acute inflammation of the gallbladder wall. Inflammation usually starts without infection, although secondary infection can follow.

While estrogen use is a risk factor, long term use of combined continuous hormone therapy ((after 5.6 years' use: from 27 per 1000 to between 38 and 60 per 1000) and estrogen only hormone therapy (after 7 years' use: from 27 per 1000 to between 38 and 60 per 1000) cause gallbladder disease.

AAC usually develops in critically ill or injured patients. The risk factors include age (>50 years), surgery, trauma, diabetes mellitus, and prolonged use of parental nutrition.Shock or cardiac arrest has also been associated with AAC.

In the Liraglutide Effect and Action in Diabetes: Evaluation of Cardiovascular Outcome Results (LEADER) trial on diabetic patients, liragulutide use was associated with an increased risk of acute gallbladder or biliary disease vs placebo (HR = 1.60).

A systematic review and meta-analysis of 76 RCTs with 103,371 patients found that use of GLP-1 receptor agonists was associated with increased risk of cholecystitis (RR, 1.36; 95% CI, 1.14-1.62) especially when used at higher doses, for longer durations, and for weight loss.

In a retrospective analysis of 601,665 admissions for acute cholecystitis in Japan showed ambient temperature may play a role. High temperature (≥10.0 °C) and low temperature (<5.0 °C) were associated with increased admission for acute cholecystitis.
Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors increased the risk of cholecystitis in a network meta-anaylsis involving 82 RCTs, especially with a longer treatment duration.

Cystic duct obstruction from gallstones or their passage into the gallbladder neck causes acute inflammation of the gallbladder wall. The impacted gallstone causes biliary distension with subsequent compromise in blood flow and lymphatic drainage to the gallbladder, resulting in mucosal ischemia and necrosis.Degree and duration of obstruction are the factors that determine progression to AC.

Infection of the gallbladder subsequently develops in 47% to 100% of patients. Bacteria causing secondary infection include Escherichia coli, Klebsiella organisms, Enterococci, Pseudomonas organisms, and Bacteroides fragilis.
The clinical signs and symptoms of right upper quadrant pain, mass, tenderness along with systemic signs of fever helps one to suspect AC. B
Ultrasound is the best initial diagnostic test. B
Scintigraphy with HIDA can be obtained if ultrasound results are negative or equivocal or in a patient without fever or elevated WBC but with gallstones. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Burning or gnawing epigastric pain, possible epigastric tenderness on examination, positive Helicobacter pylori stool antigen or breath test
Prodromal symptoms (eg, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, myalgias), clinical jaundice, positive serologic markers
Upper abdominal pain radiating to back, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, fever; elevated serum lipase
Biliary pain, jaundice, spiking fever; possible bacteremia, shock; positive endoscopic retrograde cholangio-pancreatography (ERCP)
Fever, costovertebral tenderness, nausea, vomiting, positive nitrate and leukocyte esterase in the urine dipstick test
Heartburn (substernal burning pain) aggravated by certain foods or body positions; normal examination
Crampy abdominal pain that is chronic and often associated with defecation or change in stool frequency or appearance
Chest pain (rarely sharp or burning), may radiate to upper epigastrium, shoulder, upper arm, or neck; ECG changes or elevated cardiac enzymes are typically seen
Productive cough, fever, dyspnea, crackles in lung base, abnormal CXR
Acute pain (anywhere in the body), fever, hemolytic anemia, red cell morphology

list.listitem: Early diagnosis of acute cholecystitis is essential for prompt therapeutic decisions and prevention of complications.

Key factors include a history of gallstones and characteristic pain in the right upper quadrant (RUQ), lasting more than 3 to 5 hours, and unremitting. It is associated with fever, nausea, and/or leukocytosis. Pain rapidly increases in severity and then plateaus with occasional radiation to the tip of the right scapula. The duration of pain can be shorter if the gallstone returns into the gallbladder lumen or passes into the duodenum.

The presence of RUQ pain, Murphy sign (cessation of inspiration caused by pain during RUQ palpation on deep inspiration), and chills best predict cholecystitis. The absence of RUQ pain significantly reduces the likelihood of cholecystitis (LR− 0.28). Unfortunately, a meta-analysis found that no single clinical or laboratory finding rules in or rules out acute cholecystitis.

There are no specific blood tests for acute cholecystitis (AC), but an elevated WBC count and/or CRP (>3 mg/dL) may be useful in confirming an inflammatory process. Although hepatic transaminaes, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin are not helpful, they may become elevated in the presence of common bile duct obstruction

Persistent pain (>72 hours), leukocytosis (WBC >18,000), or palpable tender mass in RUQ may indicate moderate severity, while evidence of organ damage (hypotension, altered mental status, oliguria, SCr >2mg/dL, INR >1.5, platelet <100,000) may indicate severe/complicated disease (eg, pericholecystic abscess formation, bilioenteric fistula, or gallbladder perforation with peritonitis).
CRP >15.25 mg/dl can be one of the predictive factors to diagnose gangrenous cholecystitis.

In a retrospective cohort study of 7458 patients with AC and a history of chronic cholecystitis, a National Surgical Quality Improvement Program database showed abnormal hepatic transaminases is a positive predictor for CBD stones.

Systemic inflammation markers such as neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) and thrombocyte-lymphocyte ratio can be used to predict the risk of complicated acute cholecystitis.In a systemic review an NLR > 2.9 was an independent predictor of cholecystitis (OR 36.0, p = 0.006). In simple versus severe cholecystitis, an NLR cut-off value of 8.5 was identified (AUC = 0.73)..
Ischemia modified albumin (IMA), a marker of hypoperfusion and oxidative stress, could be useful in predicting the clinical severity of acute cholecystitis.
Blood culture should be obtained for patients with grade 3 cholecystitis (odds ratio for blood stream infection 4.51) who undergo emergency cholecystectomy.

Point Of Care Ultrasound (POCUS) is reliable for the diagnosis of acute cholecystitis. The sensitivity and specificity of POCUS to diagnose cholecystitis was 67.1% (95% CI 54.9-77.9%) and 97.6% (95% CI 95.9-98.8%) respectively. The negative predictive value was 95.6% (95% CI 93.9-96.8%).

In a prospective observational validation study of 153 patients, the Bedside Sonographic Acute Cholecystitis (SAC) Score using POCUS is useful in diagnosis of acute cholecystitis. A low Bedside SAC Score < 2 (sensitivity of 100%) rules out AC and patients with a high Bedside SAC Score ≥ 7 (specificity of 95.7%) rule in for AC.

Imaging studies are essential for the diagnosis. Right upper quadrant ultarsound should be ordered first. Scintigraphy with can be obtained in a symptomatic patient if ultrasound results are negative or equivocal or in a patient without fever or an elevated WBC but with gallstones. Nonvisualization by HIDA scan in a patients with localized RUQ pain, elevated WBC, and fever establishes the diagnosis. The HIDA scan is useful for diagnosis of both calculous cholecystitis and acalculous cholecystitis.
Distention of both length and width of gallbladder on point of care Ultrasound is more specific with acute over chronic cholecystitis; OR 4.32 (95% CI 1.42-13.14) in a small retrospective study.

In a meta-analysis of 10 studies, emergency physician-performed point-of-care ultrasound with final diagnosis as the reference standard (7 studies, n=1,772) had a pooled sensitivity of 70.9% (95% confidence interval [CI] 62.3 to 78.2), specificity of 94.4% (95% CI 88.2 to 97.5), positive likelihood ratio of 12.7 (5.8 to 27.5), and negative likelihood ratio of 0.31 (0.23 to 0.41) for the diagnosis of acute cholecystitis.

Patients with acute RUQ pain but no fever and a normal WBC should undergo either an abdominal ultrasound or CT scan. CT findings compatible with AC include gallstones, gallbladder distention, gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fat stranding or fluid, and adjacent liver enhancement. Detection of gallstones alone does not definitively diagnose acute cholecystitis. Multidetector computed tomography findings can distinguish AC from Chronic Cholecystitis. .

Follow up US subsequent to CT in subjects with suspecious AC, increases the PPV in low confidence CT findings, on the otherhand it adds little value in high confidence positive CT(PPV of CT was 44.7% without US and 50.5% when US was positive).

Radiographic demonstration of gas in the gallbladder wall, lumen, or pericholecystic tissues indicates emphysematous cholecystitis (a severe variant of AC). This is more common in patients with diabetes mellitus and in older patients.
In patients with AC, an algorithm using non-binary ultrasound and clinical assessments had higher sensitivity, higher diagnostic rate, and fewer adverse outcomes, than radiologist impressions.

A clinical decision rule has been developed and validated to predict the likelihood of common bile duct stones. Age > 55 years, pancreatitis, cholangitis, cirrhosis, alkaline phosphatase level of 125 - 250 or > 250 U/L, total bilirubin level > 4 mg/dL, common bile duct size > 6 mm, and common bile duct stone detection are the predictors.
Suspect cholecystitis in patients who present with RUQ pain, fever, abdominal tenderness, and Murphy sign. No single finding is very reliable, though, particularly in older patients.

The initial diagnostic test is an Ultrasound. Scintigraphy with HIDA can be obtained if ultrasound results are equivocal. The findings of stones on imaging combined with physical and/or laboratory signs of localized inflammation in the RUQ suggest AC.
See for a suggested approach to treatment.
Opioids, such as morphine, hydromorphone, or meperidine, are appropriate therapy for acute pain relief in patients with acute cholecystitis, although ketorolac is prefered for biliary colic. A
Early cholecystectomy (within 72 hours) is the definitive treatment of choice for acute cholecystitis. A
Open cholecystectomy may be appropriate for patients with cirrhosis, a gallbladder mass, extensive upper abdominal surgery, or suspicion of malignancy, or in late third trimester of pregnancy. C
High-risk patients (eg, critically ill, poor surgical candidates) may benefit from emergent percutaneous cholecystostomy. C,
Opiate analgesia can be used for pain control during evaluation. Although its use can alter the physical examination findings, it does not increase the risk .

In one RCT, 75% of patients with uncomplicated gallstones (managed with analgesia and monitoring) did not require surgery over the ensuing 18 months. Without evidence of CBD blockage or acute pancreatitis, there is no need to rush to surgery.
Antibiotics (eg, ureidopenicillin, third-generation cephalosporins) can be the initial therapy along with IV fluids and analgesics NSAIDs). Most patients will improve within 12 to 24 hours.

There is no convincing evidence for a protective role of bile salt therapy against biliary complications such as AC; there is also no benefit from bile salts in patients with symptomatic gallstones awaiting cholecystectomy.
Perioperative dexamethasone was shown in one RCT to reduce nausea following elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy (8% vs. 27%; NNT = 5.3).

In a meta-analysis of 3 RCTs, single dose of prophylactic antibiotics in patients underoging acute laparoscopic cholecystectomy for mild to moderate acute cholecystitis does not offer benefit in reducing the infective complications.

However, a multicenter randomized non-inferiority clinical trial with 226 patients found a lower rate of complications in patients randomized to 2 gm cefazolin preoperatively (7.1% vs 12.6%) in patients being treated for for mild to moderate acute cholecystitis.

Patients with acute cholecystitis who have a high probability of having bactibilia (eg, common duct stones, emergency surgery, intraoperative findings, age over 70 years) are at risk for developing postoperative infection and should receive a single dose of prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotic immediately before surgery (typically a second- or third-generation cephalosporin).

A randomized controlled trial enrolled 414 patients having surgery for calculous cholecystitis, all of whom had pre-operative antibiotics,found that the addition of postoperative amoxicillin-clavulanic acid 3 times a day for 5 days did not reduce the likelihood of post-operative infection (15% vs. 17%, p = NS).
No significant difference was observed between single and combined use of antibiotics for prophyaxis or therapeutic purposes, in terms of treatment effectiveness and hospitalization duration.
See algorithm in for an overview of treatment.

Early cholecystectomy (within 72 hours) is the definitive first line treatment of choice for AC since recurrent symptomatic gallbladder inflammation often occurs despite medical therapy. This can be performed by laparoscopy or laparotomy (ie, open approach).
Early cholecystectomy in patients with sickle cell disease with uncomplicated cholecystitis has better outcome than patients who has advance clinical presenation.

A meta-analysis of 28 studies showed early laparascopic cholecystectomy is more cost effectice than delayed laparascopic cholecystectomy in the treatment of AC with an incremental net benefit of US$1221 (US$187 to US$2255) in high income countries..

Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy is associated with a significant reduction in hospital stay (6-8 vs. 11-12 days for delayed group) and decreases the rate of recurrent gallstone-related complication in patients with mild gallstone pancreatitis, but does not significantly affect conversion rate to open cholecystectomy. Compared with laparoscopic cholecystectomy, robotic-assisted cholecystectomy was associated with a higher rate of bile duct injury necessitating a definitive operative repair within 1 year (0.7% vs 0.2%; relative risk [RR], 3.16 [95% CI, 2.57-3.75] in one cohort study. Robot-assisted surgery is safe but no more effective than human-assisted surgery.
Analysis of a multicenter evaluation of cholecystitis database showed laparoscopic cholecystectomy regardless of when it is performed in the day.

Conversion to an open procedure may be required for significant adhesions, inflammation, difficulty delineating the anatomy, or significant bleeding. The conversion rate in a case series of 1083 patients was 2.2%.
Open cholecystectomy may be appropriate for patients with cirrhosis, a gallbladder mass, extensive upper abdominal surgery, of suspicion of malignancy, or late third trimester of pregnancy.

In a retrospective case control study of 320 patients with AC, preoperative clinical data such as older age, male sex, gallbladder wall thickness, and pericholecystic fluid are identifed as higher risk of conversion to open cholecystectomy.
Gallbladders with severe inflammation have a longer operating time and increased risks of complicaitons. The Parkland grading scale stratifies the GB inflammation using intraoperative images.

Patients with typical biliary colic symptoms without gallstones and markedly high ejection fraction by biliary scintigraphy scan (HIDA) might benefit from having cholecystectomy to alleviate their symptoms.
A systemic review and 2 meta-analysis showed prophylactic drainage after laparascopic cholecystectomy is not helpful to reduce the complication to treat AC.
Laparascopic surgery with 3-dimensional models using a new digital holographic image technology is feasible and its efficacy depend on experience of the surgeon.
Implementation of an early recovery program after early cholecystectomy for acute cholecystitis decreased the length of stay and did not increase the morbidity rate.
Incentive spirometry decreased the severity of shoulder tip pain after laparascopic cholecystectomy with no complications.

In a study of 200 patients with calculus AC, Intraperitoneal normal saline instillation following laparoscopic cholecystectomy may be a choice for reducing postoperative pain thus improving patients' experience.
Combination of ultrasonography and biliary scintiscan can accurately predict bile duct calculi and could be used as a guide for selective cholangiography.

Among 92,932 patients undergoing cholecystectomy, the use of intraoperative cholangiography was not associated with a higher rate of common bile duct injury (0.21% with cholangiography and 0.36% without).
Routine use of ICG- fluorescence cholangiography did not make any difference in conversion or complication rate during laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
Emergency Laparaoscopic Cholecystectomy:

Emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy was associated with increased incidences of multitude of operation-related adverse outcomes such as subtotal cholecystectomy (OR 1.94; P = .011), bile leak (OR 2.38; P = .013), intraoperative drains (OR 2.54; P < .001), prolonged postoperative length of stay (OR 7.26; P < .001), postoperative imaging (OR 1.83, P = .006), and postoperative readmission (OR 1.90; P = .005).
However, immediate surgery is indicated for gangrenous cholecystitis or perforation with peritonitis.

Percutaneous cholecystomy should be considered in certain critically ill and/or at very high surgical risk (eg, Child-Pugh class C cirrhosis) if they fail to respond to medical managment, because of high risk of liver failure and heavy hemorrhage due to surgery. Clinical improvement occurs in 80% to 90% of patients within 3 to 5 days after cholecystotomy.

A study on 163 patients diagnosed with acute calculous cholecystitis and treated with percutaneous cholecystostomy recommends duration of catheter should be minimum 21 days to reduce the rate of recurrence.

In general, keep cholecystostomy tubes in place until the patient's general condition improves, the bile output decreases, and the cystic duct is patent. Patients can be discharged with this tube in place.

In a retrospective clinical analysis to evaluate the timing of laparoscopic cholecystectomy after percutaneous transhepatic gallbladder drainage (PTGBD), laparoscopic cholecystectomy is recommended within 1 week after gallbladder drainage surgery for all non-elderly patients diagnosed with acute moderate to severe cholecystitis with an anesthesia risk score [American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA)] ≤2.
Laparascopic subtotal cholecystectomy is a safe and feasible option after percutaneous transhepatic gallbladder drainage for grade II or III acute cholecystitis (AC).

A systemic review of 19 studies (13340 patients) to clarify the best laparoscopic subtotal cholecystectomy technique for finalizing a difficult cholecystectomy indicates that closure of the gallbladder stump represents the best method to avoid complications.

A meta-analysis of 10 studies showed subtotal cholecystectomy significantly lowered the risk for CBD injury (0 ​% vs. 1.6 ​%, RR 0.30, 95%CI 0.10-0.87) but increased risk of bile leaks (RR 3.5, 95%CI 1.79-6.84), postoperative ERCP (RR 2.86, 95%CI 1.53-5.35), intraabdominal collections (RR 2.55, 95%CI 1.32-4.93), and reoperation (RR 2.92, 95%CI 1.14-7.47).

Laparoscopic fenestrating subtotal cholecystectomy and reconstituing subtotal cholecystectomy techniques are associated with a higher rate of bile leaks and reconstituing subtotal cholecystectomy has more long term morbidty as compared to total cholecystectomy.

Gall bladder drainage can be another option for symptomatic GB disease. In high risk individuals, endoscopic ultrasound guided gallbladder drainage (EUS-GBD) resulted in higher technical and clinical success rates [OR 3.91 (95% CI 1.52-10.09); P = 0.005 and OR 4.59 (95% CI 1.84-11.46); P = 0.001] and lower recurrence rate [OR 0.17 (95% CI 0.06-0.52); P = 0.002 compared to ERC assisted transpapillary drainage.

Endoscopic procedures (nasogallbladder drainage and gallbladder stenting) can also be used to achieve gallbladder drainage with similar success and complication rates compared to the percutaneous approach, although data are limited. EUS guided GB drianage as well as EUS guided bile duct drainage are promising alternatives, provided high technical success and acceptable clinical success in an another study.

Clinical success is probably equivalent according to the study on trial sequential analysis of EUS guided GB drainage vs percutaneous cholecystostomy in patients with acute cholecystitis. PTGBD can provide superior technical success and EUS-GBD has decreased overall adverse effects and unplanned readmission.
Endoscopic ultrasound guided naso-gallbladder drainage may be a good option for the treatment of self expandable metalic stent related cholecystitis in patients with malignant biliary obstruction.

A meta-analysis of delayed laparascopic cholecystectomy after percutaneous transhepatic gallbladder drainage (PTGBSD) vs emergency laparascopic cholecystectomy showed PTGBD has significant better effect on intraoperative bleeding, conversion rate to open surgery, postoperative complications, bile leakage, bile duct injury, and wound infection . The only drawback on PTGBD group was longer hospital stay.

A study comparing laparascopic cholecystectomy outcomes after PTGBD between 208 patients with PTGBD tube preservation versus removal, showed the surgical outcome may be inferior when the drainage tube is preserved rather than removed before laparascopic cholecystectomy when it is performed > 12 days after PTGBD.
In an observational study of 132 patients with acute cholecystitis who underwent successful PTGBD duration of three days or less of antibacterial therapy may be adequate .

In another observation study of 1,725 extremely ill patients diagnosed with acute acalculous cholecystitis, "bridge therapy" with percutaneous cholecystostomy was associated with lower morbidity (5% vs. 8%), fewer ICU admissions (28% vs. 35%), decreased length-of-stay (7 vs. 8 days) and lower overall costs when compared to initial treatment with either laparoscopic or open cholecystectomy.

However, in a randomized controlled trial 142 high risk patients (APACHE II Score >6) laparoscopic cholecystectomy was superior to percutaneous catheter drainage with regards to major complications (12% vs 65%), reintervention rates (12% vs 66%), recurrent biliary disease (5% vs 53%) and length of stay (5 days vs 9 days) but had no effect on mortality.

Endoscopic transpapillary gallbladder stenting prevented recurrent cholecystitis (0% vs 18.3% at 3 months, 0% vs 10% at 6 months) in acute cholecystitis patients with common bile duct stone whose cholecystectomy was deferred for 3 months in a RCT involving 120 patients.

Surgical Infection Society recommend use of peri-operative antibiotic agents for patients undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy for AC and maximum of 4 days of antibiotic agents in patients undergoing cholecystectomy for severe (Tokyo Guidelines grade III) cholecystitis.

In a small study of 150 patients with acute calculous cholecystitis undergoing cholecystectomy, infectious complications within 30 days of operation did not differ between groups (4% in each) recieving a single preoperative dose of 2000 mg cefazolin or intravenous cefuroxime 750 mg plus metronidazole 500 mg, three times daily, plus the preoperative antibiotic.

In a nonblinded RCT of 414 patients presenting with mild to moderate calculous cholecystitis requiring cholecystectomy, all of whom recieved 2 days of preoperative antibiotics, there was no difference in postoperative infection rates in those who were randomized to stop antibiotics postoperatively vs. those who continued antibiotics for 5 days postoperatively (17% vs. 15%).
A comprehensive cohort of 289,627 patients going through sleeve gastrectomy or gastric bypass surgery, the complications rate was high with comcomitant cholecystectomy, hence it should be avoided.
Gallbladder aspiration can also be considered in patients at high surgical risk. The success rates in single PGBA and repetitive PGBA (2–4 times) were 50% to 93% and 76% to 96%, respectively.

Optimal duration of antibiotic use postoperatively in acute cholecystitis is unknown; historically the antibiotic is usually continued until the patient is afebrile and the WBC is within normal limits.

A sytematic review of 4 RCTs with 953 total patients found that in patients undergoing emergency cholecystectomy for acute calculous cholecystitis, prolonged use of postoperative antibiotics did not improve the post-operative outcome (infectious and non-infectious), when compared to no antibiotics group. ( P= NS).
Complications include progression to gangrenous gallbladder, gallbladder perforation, empyema, abscess formation, and common bile duct obstruction.
These conditions typically require emergency decompression of the gallbladder or cholecystectomy.

Systemic review of studies that described the managment of GB perforation, open cholecystectomy has a lower rate of addiitonal surgical procedure and postoperative complications, but has a longer hospital stay.

Initial therapy of AC is directed toward general support of the patient including IV fluid (eg, normal saline), no oral intake (NPO), electrolyte replacement, correction of metabolic imbalance as needed, and antibacterial therapy
Management of patients with AC, an Acute Surgical Unit (ASU) model is superior to traditional model in terms of most metrics like length of hospital stay, after hour operation rate and complications.
About 2% of asymptomatic gallstones become symptomatic each year. B
Removal of the gallbladder resolves symptoms in the vast majority of patients (75%-90%). C
Rates of surgical complications for laparoscopic cholecystectomy are: death (0.001%), hemorrhage (2.3%), conversion to open surgery (1.9%), and gallbladder perforation (0.1%).
About 2.8% of gall bladder specimens submitted after cholecystectomy for symptomatic gall stones have an incidental finding of adenocarcinoma.
Predictors for the presence of incidental gallbladder cancer include age >65, dilated bile ducts and the presence of gallbladder wall thickening.
About 2% of asymptomatic gallstones become symptomatic each year.

Untreated AC can progress to gangrene, perforation of the gallbladder, empyema, or abscess formation; these conditions typically require emergency laparotomy, which increases the morbidity and mortality associated with the disease.
Removal of the gallbladder resolves symptoms in the vast majority of patients (75%-90%).

In one study of 811 patients, emergency laparascopic cholecystectamy is associated with more perioperative morbidity (prolonged postoperative length of stay, postoperative readmission, bile leak, incidences of subtotal cholecystectomy) compared to delayed cholecystectomy.

Although obesity is a perceived risk factor during LC, similar postoperative outcomes were achieved though it may be associated with greater technical difficulty during surgery than non-obese patients.
Patients selected for Percutaneous cholecystostomy tubes (PCT) have a high mortality risk of 31.9%. Follow up cholecystectomy was performed in only in 39% at a median interval of 58 days.

Rates of surgical complications for laparoscopic cholecystectomy were difficult to find for U.S. populations. The largest study (N = 9842; Romania) reported 10 deaths (0.001%), small intraoperative rates of complications (hemorrhage 2.3%, conversion to open surgery 1.9%, and gallbladder perforation 0.1%) and tiny rates of postoperative morbidity (biliary leakage 0.006%), hemorrhage (0.002%), retained stones (0.001%), and abscess (0.001%).

Analysis on prospectively maintained database of 5675 consecutive laparoscopic cholecystectomies 0.4% had primary biliary leakage (PBL). Ligation of the cystic duct reduces the incidence of PCBL resulting from dislodged endoclips.

In one study using a Swiss database of 22,953 patients undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy, risk factors for intraoperative complications included male gender (OR = 1.16), duration of intervention (OR = 1.68 per 30 minutes), higher body weight, and less surgical experience. Postoperative complications were associated with the same factors (with the exception of surgeon experience) plus intraoperative complications, emergency surgery, risk score, and conversion to open surgery.

In a cross sectional study of a nationwide sample, women with cholecystitis were significantly less likely to die (OR = 0.75) or have complications (OR = 0.86) than age matched men. Women also had a lower length of stay (OR = .95) and lower cost (OR = .93) than men.
In an observational study,one of the objective measure of Temperature, Neutrophil count and Multi organ failure (TNM) score , helps to define the mortality risk on patients with AC.
In a retrospective study of 7013 patients who underwent cardiovascular surgery, 1% of them developed postoperative cholecystitis, about 1/2 of them are asymptomatic.
In one case series of 8 patients with cholecystitis with acute (neutrophilic) inflammation in association with gallbladder carcinoma have a shortest survival.
In a retrospective study on 2285 patients, Procalicitonin > 0.09 ng/mL at admission, could be associated to a poor surgical outcome in patients treated by laparoscopic surgery for AC.

Another retropective study of 702 critically ill patients with AC, Red cell Distribution Width (RDW) was positively associated with in-hospital mortality (OR: 1.187, 95% CI [1.049, 1.343]) short-term mortality (i.e., 30-day: HR: 1.183, 95% CI [1.080, 1.295], 90-day: HR: 1.175, 95% CI [1.089, 1.268]) and long-term (i.e., 1-year: HR:1.162, 95% CI [1.089, 1.240]) mortality.

A study investigated the suitability of Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE-II) score, American Society of Anesthesiologist (ASA) grade, and Tokyo Guidelines 2018 (TG18) grade as predictors of outcome and assessed laparoscopic cholecystectomy versus percutaneous cholecystostomy (PC) as treatment options in patients with A. It showed utilization of the TG18 grade to be more accurate in risk stratifying and predicting outcomes in patients with AC .

Follow up is required for the patients who undergo cholecystectomy within 2 weeks after discharge from the hospital. Ask the patient about presence or absence of nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain, as well as ability to tolerate oral intake. On physical examination, look for wound erythema, discharge, or pain. In addition, note any signs of jaundice; if present, determine the direct and indirect bilirubin level and order an abdominal ultrasound.

Follow-up for patients who recover and are discharged after a percutaneous cholecystostomy includes a cholangiogram through the cholecystostomy tube. If no gallstones are present and the cystic duct is patent, the tube can be removed in 6 to 8 weeks. If gallstones are present and the patient is not high risk, the patient should undergo cholecystectomy in 6 to 8 weeks. Recurrence rates without cholecystectomy are as high as 33%.
Older patients are less likely to have fever, pain, or Murphy's sign.

Acute cholecystitis in patients older than 70 years is often complicated by gallbladder necrosis and peritonitis; thus early treatment is typically indicated unless the patient is inoperable due to a high surgical risk. In such a case, percutaneous transhepatic gallbladder drainage is the treatment of choice.
Elderly patients who are undergoing cholecysectomy are at increased risk due to co morbidities.
The Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation IV (APACHE IV) scoring system showed that cholecystostomy is a safe and effective treatment for elderly high-risk patients with acute cholecystitis.

In the "oldest old" patients (age >85 years), although ELC for ACC was associated with significant morbidity and mortality such as higher 90-day mortality rate (7.6% vs 1%, p < 0.001), more total complications (40.6% vs 17.7%, p < 0.001), longer LOS (6 vs 5 days, p < 0.001), and more readmissions (6.6% vs 2.6%, p < 0.001), it is not contraindicated and seems to be safe in selected patients.
The clinical decisions on cholecystectomy in a patient aged 80 years or older can be assisted through the ACS-NSQIP model.
Acute cholecystitis is the second most common cause of acute abdomen during pregnancy (after appendicitis).

In one study, 6211 women (0.5%) were identified from databases in the state of Washington with a biliary-related diagnosis at delivery or as primary diagnosis post partum. Sixty-six percent had uncomplicated cholelithiasis, and 9% had AC.
The symptomatology of acute cholecystitis is almost identical in pregnant and nonpregnant women.

Surgery as a primary treatment has been used widely because of reduced use of medications, high recurrence rate during pregnancy (44%-92% depending on the trimester of presentation), and minimizing the development of potentially life-threatening complications (eg, perforation, sepsis, peritonitis).

Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy compared with delayed operative management, is associated with a lower risk of maternal-fetal complications (1.6% for early vs 18.4% for delayed) and is recommended during all trimesters.
If surgery is elected, laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the treatment of choice regardless of trimester. B

In a retrospective, population-based cohort study including 5759 pregnant patients with AC, surgical management compared with nonoperative management was associated with lower odds of Adever Pregnancy Outcomes across all trimesters (OR, 0.75 [95% CI, 0.63-0.87]), in T1 (OR, 0.81 [95% CI, 0.66-1.00]), in T2 (OR, 0.71 [95% CI, 0.50-1.00]), and in T3 (OR, 0.45 [95% CI, 0.28-0.70]).

Acute cholecystitis (calculous and acalculous) can occur in children. The treatment is cholecystectomy. The complicaitons of AC Pain in the RUQ and elevated WBC are the most frequent features of this disease.

The commonest indication for LC in children was cholelithiasis (68.4% in 66 studies), followed by cholecystitis (59.2% in 53 studies) in a systemic review and meta-analysis of 114 studies included 76,524 LC cases. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy appears to be safe and effective.
